los.text: Describe the clinical presentation of anaemia and link to signs and symptoms and relevant investigation findings.
los.html:
• Anaemia: Hb below the reference range (WHO: <130 g/L men, <120 g/L non-pregnant women).
    • Symptoms depend on severity, speed of onset (chronic anaemia is well tolerated through compensation: ↑ cardiac output, ↑ 2,3-DPG) and cardiorespiratory reserve.
Features
General symptomsFatigue, breathlessness on exertion, palpitations, headache, dizziness, reduced exercise tolerance; angina, claudication or heart failure in those with vascular disease
General signsPallor (conjunctivae, palmar creases), tachycardia, flow murmur, wide pulse pressure; high-output heart failure if severe
Iron deficiencyKoilonychia (spoon nails), angular stomatitis, glossitis, pica, hair loss; dysphagia (post-cricoid web)
B12 deficiencyLemon-yellow tinge, glossitis, peripheral neuropathy, subacute combined degeneration (loss of proprioception and vibration, UMN signs), cognitive change
HaemolysisJaundice, splenomegaly, gallstones, dark urine
Marrow failure/infiltrationInfections (neutropenia), bruising/bleeding (thrombocytopenia), lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, bone pain (myeloma)
Sickle cellPainful crises, leg ulcers
  • Linked investigations: FBC (MCV classifies), reticulocytes (marrow response), film, ferritin, B12/folate, haemolysis screen, renal function, CRP
    • then find the cause (e.g. GI tract in iron deficiency).

los.text: Describe the components and structure of bone marrow and link to the result of the blood count used clinically
los.html:
• Bone marrow components:
ComponentRole
Haematopoietic stem cells (CD34⁺)Self-renew and give rise to myeloid (red cells, granulocytes, monocytes, megakaryocytes → platelets) and lymphoid lineages
Stroma: fibroblasts, adipocytes, osteoblasts, endothelial cells, macrophagesThe niche supporting stem cells; macrophages supply iron to erythroblasts
Growth factorsEPO (kidney), TPO (liver), G-CSF, IL-3, stem cell factor
Sites
  • Adults: axial skeleton (pelvis, sternum, vertebrae, ribs, skull, proximal femur and humerus)
  • Children: all bones
  • Extramedullary (liver, spleen) when the marrow can't cope
  • FBC parameters and what they reflect:
ParameterMeaning
Hb, red cell count, haematocritOxygen-carrying capacity
MCV (80–100 fL), MCH, MCHCRed cell size and Hb content: classifies anaemia
RDWVariation in red cell size (high in iron deficiency, mixed deficiencies)
Reticulocytes (0.5–2.5%)Marrow output: high = bleeding or haemolysis; low = production failure
WCC + differential, plateletsOther lineages: pancytopenia suggests marrow failure or infiltration (or hypersplenism, B12 deficiency)
  • Leucoerythroblastic film (nucleated red cells + immature myeloid cells) = marrow infiltration (metastases, myelofibrosis, haematological malignancy).
    • Marrow is sampled by aspirate (cell morphology) and trephine (architecture) from the posterior iliac crest.

los.text: Describe the components of red cell structure in relation to red cell development, function and mechanisms of anaemia.
los.html:
• Erythropoiesis: proerythroblast
    • → normoblasts (Hb synthesis, nucleus condenses)
    • → nucleus extruded
    • → reticulocyte (residual RNA, 1–2 days in blood)
    • → mature red cell (lifespan ~120 days).
    • Needs EPO (made by peritubular cells in response to hypoxia via HIF), iron, B12 and folate (DNA synthesis), amino acids.
StructureFunction / disease link
Biconcave disc, ~7–8 µm, no nucleus or mitochondria, deformableLarge surface area, squeezes through capillaries and splenic sinusoids
Membrane cytoskeleton (spectrin, ankyrin, band 3, protein 4.1)Defects → hereditary spherocytosis (spherical cells destroyed in the spleen), elliptocytosis
Haemoglobin: 4 globin chains (HbA α₂β₂; HbA₂ α₂δ₂; HbF α₂γ₂) each with haem (protoporphyrin + Fe²⁺)O₂ transport; ↓ affinity with ↑ CO₂, H⁺, temperature, 2,3-DPG (Bohr effect); globin mutations → sickle cell, thalassaemia
Anaerobic glycolysisATP for ion pumps (pyruvate kinase deficiency → haemolysis)
Pentose phosphate pathway → NADPH → reduced glutathioneProtects against oxidation (G6PD deficiency → haemolysis with fava beans, primaquine, nitrofurantoin, sulfonamides, infection: Heinz bodies, bite cells)
  • Removal: old cells taken up by splenic macrophages; haem → bilirubin, iron recycled.
Mechanism of anaemiaExamples
Reduced productionIron, B12, folate deficiency; CKD (low EPO); anaemia of chronic disease (hepcidin); marrow failure
Ineffective productionThalassaemia, myelodysplasia, megaloblastic anaemia
Increased destruction (haemolysis)Inherited (membrane, enzyme, haemoglobin); acquired (autoimmune, MAHA, malaria, drugs, mechanical valves)
LossBleeding (GI, menstrual)
Pooling / dilutionHypersplenism, pregnancy

los.text: Describe the relevant laboratory investigation processes and results and link to the diagnosis and treatment of haematological conditions.
los.html:
TestProcess and use
FBCEDTA (purple) tube; automated analyser (impedance, flow cytometry, spectrophotometry for Hb)
Blood film
  • Stained smear: microcytic hypochromic cells
  • Pencil cells (iron deficiency)
  • Target cells (thalassaemia, liver disease)
  • Spherocytes (hereditary spherocytosis, autoimmune haemolysis)
  • Schistocytes (MAHA: DIC, HUS, TTP)
  • Sickle cells
  • Howell–Jolly bodies (hyposplenism)
  • Hypersegmented neutrophils (megaloblastic)
  • Blasts (leukaemia)
  • Rouleaux (myeloma)
  • Teardrop cells (myelofibrosis)
Reticulocyte countMarrow response
HaematinicsFerritin (iron stores; acute-phase protein, so falsely normal in inflammation), transferrin saturation, serum iron, TIBC; B12, folate
Haemolysis screen↑ LDH, ↑ unconjugated bilirubin, ↓ haptoglobin, ↑ reticulocytes, urinary haemosiderin; DAT (Coombs) for antibody-mediated haemolysis
Hb electrophoresis / HPLCThalassaemia (raised HbA₂ in β-thal trait), sickle cell
OthersG6PD assay, intrinsic factor antibodies, coeliac serology (tTG), myeloma screen, coagulation, bone marrow, flow cytometry, cytogenetics
ResultDiagnosisTreatment
Low MCV, ferritin <30 µg/LIron deficiencyOral iron; find the cause (GI investigation in men and postmenopausal women, coeliac screen)
High MCV, low B12, IF antibodies positivePernicious anaemiaIM hydroxocobalamin lifelong
Normocytic, ↑ retics, ↑ LDH, ↓ haptoglobin, DAT positiveAutoimmune haemolytic anaemiaSteroids, rituximab
Low MCV, normal ferritin, ↑ HbA₂β-thalassaemia traitReassure, genetic counselling; no iron

los.text: Apply the pharmacology of drugs used to treat anaemia and relevant evidence for their benefits to be able to choose and manage effective treatment for individual patients
los.html:
DrugPharmacologyUse and evidenceAdverse effects / notes
Oral iron (ferrous sulfate 200 mg = 65 mg elemental iron; fumarate, gluconate)Fe²⁺ absorbed in the duodenum via DMT1; hepcidin limits absorption for ~24 h after a dose
  • Iron deficiency: once daily or alternate days (alternate-day dosing improves fractional absorption)
  • Expect Hb ↑ ~20 g/L in 3–4 weeks
  • Continue 3 months after Hb normalises to refill stores
  • GI upset, constipation or diarrhoea, black stools
  • Absorption ↑ with vitamin C, ↓ with tea, calcium, antacids, PPIs
  • Reduces absorption of levothyroxine, tetracyclines, quinolones
  • Toxic in overdose (children)
IV iron (ferric carboxymaltose, ferric derisomaltose, iron sucrose)Iron–carbohydrate complex taken up by macrophagesOral intolerance or failure, malabsorption (IBD), CKD on ESA, rapid repletion before surgery, late pregnancy, heart failure with iron deficiencyHypersensitivity (observe), hypophosphataemia (carboxymaltose), skin staining if extravasated
Hydroxocobalamin (B12)Cofactor for methionine synthase (DNA synthesis, myelin)
  • Pernicious anaemia: 1 mg IM three times a week for 2 weeks (alternate days until improvement if neurological), then every 2–3 months for life
  • Oral cyanocobalamin for dietary deficiency
Hypokalaemia at start of treatment in severe anaemia; treat B12 before folate (folate alone can worsen subacute combined degeneration)
Folic acidDNA synthesisDeficiency: 5 mg daily for 4 months; haemolytic anaemias; pregnancy 400 µg (5 mg if high risk)Check B12 first
ESAs (epoetin, darbepoetin)Recombinant EPO stimulates erythroid progenitorsAnaemia of CKD after iron repletion (target Hb 100–120 g/L), some chemotherapyHypertension, thrombosis, stroke with high Hb targets (TREAT, CHOIR trials), pure red cell aplasia
Red cell transfusionReplaces red cellsRestrictive threshold Hb <70 g/L (80 in ACS) (NICE NG24; trials TRICC, FOCUS showed restrictive is as safe)See ICM LOs
OthersHydroxycarbamide (↑ HbF in sickle cell), immunosuppression (AIHA), iron chelation (desferrioxamine, deferasirox) for transfusional iron overload, HIF-PH inhibitors (roxadustat)

los.text: Describe the physiology and pathology of haemopoiesis linked to the cause and treatment of anaemia.
los.html:
Haemopoiesis
  • a hierarchy from stem cells in the marrow niche
  • → progenitors
  • → mature cells, regulated by growth factors (EPO from kidney via hypoxia-inducible factor, TPO from liver, G-CSF, interleukins) and nutrients.
Iron regulation
  • Hepcidin (liver) degrades ferroportin, blocking iron absorption and release from macrophages.
  • Inflammation (IL-6) raises hepcidin → anaemia of chronic disease (low serum iron and TIBC, normal or high ferritin)
  • Iron deficiency, hypoxia and ineffective erythropoiesis lower hepcidin (→ iron overload in thalassaemia).
PathologyMechanismExample and treatment
Nutrient deficiency
  • Iron: too little haem → small pale cells
  • B12/folate: impaired DNA synthesis → nuclear–cytoplasmic asynchrony → large cells (megaloblastic), ineffective erythropoiesis
Replace the nutrient; treat the cause
Low EPOCKD → normocytic anaemiaESA after iron repletion
Stem cell failure
  • Aplastic anaemia (autoimmune, drugs, viruses, radiation): pancytopenia, hypocellular marrow
  • Parvovirus B19 → transient red cell aplasia (aplastic crisis in haemolytic disorders)
Transfusion, ATG + ciclosporin, stem cell transplant
Clonal / dysplasticMyelodysplasia: older patients, macrocytosis, cytopenias, risk of AMLTransfusion, azacitidine, transplant if fit
Marrow infiltrationLeukaemia, lymphoma, myeloma, metastases (breast, prostate, lung), myelofibrosis (teardrop cells, dry tap, splenomegaly)Treat the underlying disease
Globin chain imbalanceThalassaemia: ineffective erythropoiesis → marrow expansion (frontal bossing), extramedullary haemopoiesis, hepatosplenomegalyTransfusion + chelation, transplant

los.text: List the key sources of information (e.g., clinical indicators, laboratory results, patient history) necessary to support the decision to transfuse
sessions: Making a decision to transfuse, pre-transfusion blood sampling and transfusion adverse event
los.html:
SourceExamples
ClinicalSymptoms (breathlessness, chest pain, dizziness), haemodynamic status, active bleeding, comorbidities (cardiovascular disease, ACS), age, planned surgery
LaboratoryHb and its trend, platelets, coagulation, fibrinogen, haematinics (treat iron, B12 or folate deficiency instead of transfusing where possible), reticulocytes
Patient historyCause of anaemia, previous transfusions and reactions, red cell antibodies, special requirements, pregnancy
Patient viewsConsent, beliefs (e.g. Jehovah's Witnesses usually refuse blood), advance decisions
Thresholds (NICE NG24)Restrictive: transfuse if Hb <70 g/L, aim 70–90; ACS: <80 g/L, aim 80–100; individual thresholds for chronic transfusion-dependent anaemia
  • Practice: in non-bleeding adults give one unit at a time and reassess (symptoms and Hb)
    • consider alternatives (oral/IV iron, tranexamic acid, cell salvage)
    • identify special requirements (irradiated components after stem cell transplant, Hodgkin lymphoma or purine analogues such as fludarabine; CMV-negative in pregnancy and neonates)
    • document the indication.

los.text: Explain the indications for transfusion and provide supporting written information to the patient to ensure informed consent
sessions: Making a decision to transfuse, pre-transfusion blood sampling and transfusion adverse event
los.html:
ComponentMain indications
Red cellsSymptomatic anaemia below threshold, acute blood loss/major haemorrhage, peri-operative, chronic transfusion (thalassaemia, MDS)
PlateletsBleeding with thrombocytopenia; prophylaxis if count <10 × 10⁹/L (marrow failure); before procedures
FFPBleeding with coagulopathy (major haemorrhage)
CryoprecipitateFibrinogen <1.5 g/L in major haemorrhage
Valid consent(SaBTO)
  • Explain the reason
  • Benefits
  • Risks (reactions: fever, allergy; TACO; TRALI; wrong blood; infection risk very low; vCJD theoretical)
  • Alternatives
  • and the right to refuse
  • Give the written leaflet (NHS Blood and Transplant)
  • Document the discussion.
Afterwards
  • Patients who have been transfused can't donate blood
  • Anyone transfused without prior consent (e.g. in theatre or an emergency) must be told before discharge.

los.text: Complete the transfusion chart accurately, ensuring all required details are provided in line with hospital policy
sessions: Making a decision to transfuse, pre-transfusion blood sampling and transfusion adverse event
los.html:
On the transfusion prescription
Patient identifiers: full name, DOB, hospital/NHS number (must match the wristband)
Component (red cells, platelets, FFP, cryoprecipitate), number of units or volume
  • Rate/duration: red cells usually over 90–120 minutes per unit in a stable patient (faster in bleeding)
  • Each unit must finish within 4 hours of leaving controlled storage
  • Platelets and FFP ~30 minutes per unit (FFP dose ~15 mL/kg)
Special requirements (irradiated, CMV-negative)
Indication, date, prescriber's signature
Additional medicines, e.g. furosemide with each unit if at risk of TACO (elderly, heart failure, renal failure, low weight)
  • Rules: use a dedicated line (only 0.9% sodium chloride may be used with blood)
    • a blood giving set with filter
    • follow hospital policy and the TACO risk assessment.

los.text: Perform positive patient identification procedures and ensure accurate and complete documentation is maintained for transfusion
sessions: Making a decision to transfuse, pre-transfusion blood sampling and transfusion adverse event
los.html:
• Positive patient identification at every stage (most serious incidents are wrong blood in tube or wrong blood to wrong patient):
StageAction
Sampling
  • Ask the patient to state their full name and date of birth (open questions), check against the wristband and request
  • Label at the bedside, one patient at a time, never pre-label
  • Two separate samples at different times for first-time patients ("two-sample rule")
CollectionCheck the component against the patient's details
Bedside administration
  • Two checks: patient ID (stated + wristband) against the compatibility label and prescription
  • Blood group compatibility, unit number, expiry, special requirements
  • Inspect the bag (leaks, clots, discolouration)
Observations
  • Temperature, pulse, BP, RR before each unit (within 60 min), 15 minutes after starting, and at the end
  • Observe for reactions throughout (especially the first 15 min)
Documentation
  • Unit number, start and end times, staff names, observations, any reaction
  • Traceability is a legal requirement (Blood Safety and Quality Regulations 2005; records kept 30 years)

los.text: Recognise signs of transfusion reactions, identify potential causes, and take appropriate action to manage and resolve the reaction
sessions: Making a decision to transfuse, pre-transfusion blood sampling and transfusion adverse event
los.html:
ReactionTiming / featuresCauseAction
Acute haemolyticMinutes: fever, loin/chest pain, hypotension, haemoglobinuria, DIC, sense of doomABO incompatibility (wrong blood)
  • Stop
  • Keep line open with saline
  • ABCDE
  • Check ID
  • Return the unit
  • Bloods (FBC, DAT, U&E, LFT, coagulation, repeat group)
  • Urine
  • Fluids
  • ICU
Febrile non-haemolyticFever, rigors, otherwise wellCytokines, anti-leucocyte antibodiesPause/slow, paracetamol, observe
AllergicUrticaria, itchPlasma proteinsAntihistamine (chlorphenamine), continue slowly if mild
AnaphylaxisHypotension, bronchospasm, angioedemae.g. anti-IgA in IgA deficiencyStop, IM adrenaline 0.5 mg, ABCDE
TACOBreathlessness, hypertension, raised JVP, pulmonary oedemaVolume overload (elderly, heart/renal failure)Stop, sit up, oxygen, furosemide; leading cause of transfusion-related death
TRALIWithin 6 h: hypoxia, bilateral infiltrates, hypotension, feverDonor anti-HLA/HNA antibodiesStop, supportive care/ICU; no diuretics
Bacterial contaminationHigh fever, rigors, shock (especially platelets: stored at room temperature)Infected unitStop, cultures (patient and unit), broad-spectrum antibiotics
Delayed haemolytic5–10 days: anaemia, jaundice, positive DATPrevious sensitisationAntibody screen, monitor
OthersTransfusion-associated GvHD (prevent by irradiation), post-transfusion purpura, iron overload (chronic transfusion)
  • General approach: STOP the transfusion
    • ABCDE
    • check patient ID against the unit
    • call a doctor
    • treat
    • keep the bag and giving set
    • inform the lab
    • document
    • report to SHOT (and MHRA SABRE if serious).

los.text: Take a comprehensive history from a patient presenting with fatigue, including relevant medical, social, and psychological factors
sessions: Tired All The Time, Frailty history
los.html:
AreaQuestions
The fatigue
  • Duration
  • Onset
  • Pattern (worse in the morning, after exertion: post-exertional malaise)
  • Sleepiness vs weakness vs low energy
  • Effect on daily life and work
SleepQuantity, quality, snoring/witnessed apnoeas (OSA: Epworth score), shift work
MoodLow mood, anhedonia, anxiety, stress, suicidal thoughts (PHQ-9, GAD-7)
Systems review
  • Weight loss, night sweats, fever, lumps
  • Breathlessness, palpitations
  • Bleeding (menorrhagia, GI)
  • Thirst, polyuria
  • Cold intolerance, weight gain
  • Bowel change
  • Joint pain, rash
  • Muscle weakness
Past medicalCKD, heart failure, COPD, diabetes, cancer, autoimmune disease
DrugsBeta-blockers, antihistamines, opioids, benzodiazepines, antidepressants, statins; alcohol, recreational drugs, caffeine
SocialWork, caring roles, finances, relationships, domestic abuse, diet (vegan: B12, iron), exercise
Gynae/otherMenstrual history, pregnancy, travel, sexual history (HIV, hepatitis)
ICEWhat do they think is causing it? What worries them?

los.text: Explain the importance of conducting a thorough systems review when managing non-specific symptoms like fatigue, to ensure all potential causes are considered
sessions: Tired All The Time, Frailty history
los.html:
Fatigue is non-specificAlmost any physical or psychological illness can cause it, so the systems review is often where the diagnosis appears (e.g. menorrhagia → iron deficiency; thirst → diabetes or hypercalcaemia; snoring → OSA; joint stiffness → PMR).
Why it matters
  • Picks up red flags (weight loss, night sweats, lymphadenopathy, bleeding: cancer, lymphoma, TB)
  • Avoids anchoring or diagnostic overshadowing (attributing everything to stress, depression or age)
  • Identifies multiple contributors in multimorbidity
  • Targets investigations rather than a scattergun approach
  • and reassures the patient they've been taken seriously.
  • First-line tests guided by it: FBC, U&E, LFT, TFTs, HbA1c, ferritin, CRP/ESR, calcium, coeliac serology, urine dip
  • Then B12/folate, CK, vitamin D, HIV, myeloma screen, cortisol if indicated.

los.text: Discuss key differential diagnoses for fatigue, incorporating the concept of frailty and how it impacts diagnosis and management
sessions: Tired All The Time, Frailty history
los.html:
CategoryDifferentials for fatigue
HaematologicalAnaemia (iron, B12, folate), myeloma, lymphoma, leukaemia
Endocrine/metabolicHypothyroidism, diabetes, hypercalcaemia, Addison's, hypopituitarism, vitamin D deficiency
Organ failureCKD, heart failure, COPD, liver disease
InfectionPost-viral, EBV, TB, HIV, hepatitis, endocarditis
MalignancyAny
InflammatoryRA, SLE, polymyalgia rheumatica, IBD, coeliac disease
NeurologicalMS, Parkinson's, myasthenia
SleepObstructive sleep apnoea, insomnia, shift work
PsychologicalDepression, anxiety, stress, burnout
DrugsBeta-blockers, sedatives, alcohol
ME/CFSDiagnosis of exclusion: post-exertional malaise, unrefreshing sleep, >3 months
Frailty
  • a syndrome of reduced physiological reserve making people vulnerable to minor stressors (e.g. a UTI causing delirium and immobility).
  • Assess with the Clinical Frailty Scale (1–9; ≥5 = frail), eFI, gait speed, Timed Up and Go
  • Fried phenotype (weight loss, exhaustion, weak grip, slow walking, low activity).
How frailty changes things
  • Fatigue may be part of frailty itself
  • Illness presents atypically (falls, delirium, immobility, incontinence, medication side effects: the "frailty syndromes")
  • Several causes often coexist
  • Polypharmacy
  • Balance the burden of investigation against benefit and the patient's goals
  • Comprehensive geriatric assessment (MDT), deprescribing, nutrition, strength and balance exercise, social support, advance care planning.

los.text: Interpret Full Blood Count (FBC) results in conjunction with relevant clinical information to form a clinical opinion
los.html:
ParameterTypical adult rangeHighLow
HbMen 130–180, women 115–165 g/LPolycythaemia (PV, hypoxia, smoking, dehydration)Anaemia
MCV80–100 fLSee ICM Year 2 › Haematology & fatigue › LO 10
WCC4–11 × 10⁹/LNeutrophilia: infection, steroids, inflammation, CML; lymphocytosis: viral, CLL; eosinophilia: allergy, asthma, parasites, drugsNeutropenia: drugs (carbimazole, clozapine, chemotherapy, methotrexate), viral, marrow failure, B12 deficiency
Platelets150–400 × 10⁹/LReactive (bleeding, iron deficiency, inflammation, infection, cancer), essential thrombocythaemiaITP, DIC, heparin (HIT), liver disease/alcohol, marrow failure, hypersplenism, sepsis
  • Forming an opinion: compare with previous results
    • link to symptoms and history (e.g. microcytic anaemia in a 65-year-old man = GI blood loss until proven otherwise → suspected cancer referral; macrocytosis with heavy drinking; neutropenia on carbimazole with sore throat = agranulocytosis: stop drug, urgent FBC)
    • look at all three lineages (pancytopenia → urgent haematology)
    • consider drugs, pregnancy, ethnicity (benign ethnic neutropenia).

los.text: Classify common types of anaemia (e.g., microcytic, macrocytic, normocytic) based on red cell indices from FBC results
los.html:
MCVCauses
Microcytic (<80 fL)Iron deficiency (commonest), thalassaemia trait, anaemia of chronic disease (later), sideroblastic anaemia (congenital, alcohol, lead), lead poisoning
Normocytic (80–100 fL)Acute blood loss, anaemia of chronic disease, CKD, haemolysis, marrow failure or infiltration, mixed deficiency (iron + B12), pregnancy
Macrocytic (>100 fL)
  • Megaloblastic: B12 deficiency (pernicious anaemia, gastrectomy, terminal ileal disease, vegan diet, metformin), folate deficiency (diet, alcohol, pregnancy, coeliac, methotrexate, phenytoin, trimethoprim).
  • Non-megaloblastic: alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, reticulocytosis (haemolysis, bleeding), myelodysplasia, myeloma, drugs (hydroxycarbamide, azathioprine)
  • Iron deficiency vs thalassaemia trait (both microcytic): IDA: low ferritin, high RDW, low red cell count
    • thal trait: normal ferritin, high red cell count for the Hb, Mentzer index (MCV ÷ RBC) <13, raised HbA₂ (β-thal trait).

los.text: Identify relevant additional investigations that may be required based on FBC results, clinical signs, and suspected aaetiologies of anaemia
los.html:
FBC findingNext investigations
Microcytic
  • Ferritin (<30 µg/L = iron deficiency; if inflamed, transferrin saturation <20%)
  • Then the cause: coeliac serology (tTG + total IgA)
  • Menstrual history
  • Urine dip
  • FIT (primary care)
  • OGD and colonoscopy (or CT colonography) for men and postmenopausal women
  • Hb electrophoresis if ferritin normal
Macrocytic
  • B12, folate
  • LFTs
  • GGT (alcohol)
  • TFTs
  • Reticulocytes
  • Film (hypersegmented neutrophils, target cells)
  • Intrinsic factor antibodies if B12 low
  • Coeliac serology
  • Protein electrophoresis (myeloma)
  • Bone marrow if unexplained (MDS)
Normocytic
  • Reticulocytes (high: bleeding or haemolysis; low: production)
  • U&E (CKD)
  • CRP/ESR
  • Haematinics (mixed deficiency)
  • Haemolysis screen (LDH, bilirubin, haptoglobin, DAT, film)
  • Myeloma screen (protein electrophoresis, serum free light chains, calcium)
  • TFTs
Pancytopenia, blasts, leucoerythroblastic filmUrgent haematology referral, film, bone marrow
  • Let the clinical picture guide: dyspepsia → OGD
    • change in bowel habit → colonoscopy
    • jaundice → haemolysis screen
    • bone pain or high ESR → myeloma screen
    • neuropathy → B12.
